cicd.q: Design a deployment pipeline from merge to production. Where do you put gates, and how do you roll back?
talking_points: Stages: build once, unit/integration tests, staging, progressive production rollout
Gates: automated checks plus manual approval for high-risk changes; every artifact immutable and traceable
Rollback is a forward deploy of the previous artifact; keep the old version warm and tested

cicd.q: Compare blue-green, canary, and rolling deployments. When would you pick each?
talking_points: Blue-green: instant switch, full duplicate capacity, fast rollback; expensive
Canary: small traffic slice first, catch regressions early; needs traffic-splitting and good metrics
Rolling: cheap and gradual, but slow rollback and mixed versions during the rollout

cicd.q: A deploy just caused an outage. Walk through your response.
talking_points: Mitigate first: roll back or roll forward to restore service before root-causing
Communicate status, freeze further deploys, preserve logs and evidence
Follow up with a blameless postmortem and a concrete action item on the pipeline

cicd.q: How do you keep secrets out of build logs and container images in a CI/CD pipeline?
talking_points: Inject secrets at deploy time from a secret manager; never bake them into images or repos
Mask secret values in logs; use OIDC/short-lived credentials instead of long-lived tokens
Scan images and repos for leaked credentials as a pipeline gate

kubernetes.q: A pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk through your debugging, step by step.
talking_points: kubectl describe pod for events, kubectl logs (including previous container)
Check exit codes, OOMKilled, failed probes, missing env/config/secrets
Verify image pull, resource requests vs node capacity, and application startup dependencies

kubernetes.q: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe? What happens when each fails?
talking_points: Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure removes the pod from service endpoints
Liveness for deadlocks, readiness for warmup and dependency checks
Never point liveness at a downstream dependency, or a dependency outage restarts everything

kubernetes.q: How does a rolling update work, and what happens to in-flight requests during it?
talking_points: Deployment controller replaces pods gradually, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable
Readiness gates traffic; preStop hooks and terminationGracePeriod drain in-flight requests
Without graceful shutdown and proper probes, requests die mid-flight

kubernetes.q: Explain how the scheduler decides which node a pod lands on.
talking_points: Filtering (predicates): resource requests, node selectors, taints/tolerations, affinity
Scoring (priorities): spreading, bin packing, then the best-scoring node wins
Requests drive placement; limits do not; unschedulable pods surface as Pending events

kubernetes.q: Your cluster's etcd loses quorum. What happens, and how do you recover?
talking_points: No writes to the API server: no deploys, no scaling, no pod rescheduling; running workloads keep running
Quorum math: a 3-node cluster tolerates 1 failure; 2 failures is fatal
Recover from backup or by rebuilding the quorum from a surviving member, then verify consistency

linux.q: A production host has a rising load average with high iowait. Walk through how you diagnose it.
talking_points: Use top/iostat/vmstat/sar to separate CPU, memory, and disk pressure
Identify the process and syscall pattern with strace or perf
Check disk saturation, slow filesystem, or noisy neighbors on shared storage

linux.q: What is the difference between a zombie process and an orphan process, and how does each arise?
talking_points: Zombie: exited but parent has not reaped it via wait(); occupies a PID slot
Orphan: parent exited; reparented to init/systemd which reaps it
Zombies accumulate when the parent is broken or ignores SIGCHLD

linux.q: How would you find which process is listening on TCP port 8080, and what does each step do?
talking_points: ss -tlnp or netstat -tlnp shows sockets and owning PIDs
Map PID to process with ps; check the binary, its cwd, and open files in /proc
Mention the /proc filesystem as the underlying source of truth

linux.q: `df` shows free disk space, but writes keep failing. What could cause this and how do you fix it?
talking_points: Deleted files still held open by a process: space is not reclaimed until the fd closes; find with lsof
Inode exhaustion: df -i; many small files on ext filesystems
Reserved blocks for root, quotas, or a full overlay filesystem in containers

linux.q: A cron job runs fine manually but fails under cron. How do you debug it?
talking_points: Environment differences: minimal PATH, no shell profile, different working directory
Capture stdout/stderr to a log file; check mail/spool and syslog for cron entries
Absolute paths, lock files to prevent overlap, and explicit environment setup

networking.q: Explain the TCP three-way handshake. Why three messages and not two?
talking_points: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: both sides agree on sequence numbers and connection parameters
Three messages confirm bidirectional reachability; two would leave one side unsure
Tie to SYN floods and SYN cookies as operational context

networking.q: What is the difference between a Layer 4 and a Layer 7 load balancer? When would you use each?
talking_points: L4 routes on IP/port; cheap, fast, protocol-agnostic. L7 routes on HTTP headers, paths, cookies
L7 enables content-based routing, retries, and header manipulation
L7 adds latency and TLS termination cost; L4 for raw TCP services like databases

networking.q: How does DNS resolution work end to end? What role does TTL play in incidents?
talking_points: Resolver to root to TLD to authoritative; caching at each layer
TTL controls how long bad records persist; low TTL before planned changes, high TTL for stability
Stale or poisoned cache and DNS as a hidden single point of failure

networking.q: `ping` to a host works, but the application times out. How do you debug?
talking_points: ICMP succeeding only proves L3 reachability; check TCP connect, TLS, and the app itself
Test each layer: telnet/nc to the port, curl with timing, check firewall and security groups
Look for MTU issues, half-open connections, and DNS resolving to the wrong endpoint

networking.q: What is the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy? Give an operational example of each.
talking_points: Forward proxy sits in front of clients (egress control, caching); reverse proxy sits in front of servers
Reverse proxy: TLS termination, load balancing, rate limiting at the edge
Misconfiguring one for the other is a classic source of header and routing bugs

observability.q: What are the differences between metrics, logs, and traces? Give an example where you would use each.
talking_points: Metrics: aggregated numbers over time, cheap, good for alerting and trends
Logs: discrete events with context, good for debugging a specific failure
Traces: request flow across services, good for latency and dependency analysis

observability.q: How do you decide what to page on versus what to ticket on?
observability.source: Google SRE book (Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly), alerting chapters
talking_points: Page on user-facing symptoms tied to SLOs: fast-burn error budget alerts
Ticket on slow burns and causes: things that need attention but not at 3am
Every page should be actionable; unactionable pages train people to ignore the pager

observability.q: Your alert fires, but every dashboard looks green. What do you do?
talking_points: Verify the alert is real: check the raw query, the time window, and whether it self-resolved
Look for blind spots: missing instrumentation, sampled-out errors, or the wrong aggregation
Tune the alert threshold or fix the instrumentation, and record the outcome

observability.q: What are the four golden signals, and how would you use them to debug a latency spike?
observability.source: Google SRE book (Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly), monitoring chapter
talking_points: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Start with latency and errors to scope the blast radius, then saturation to find the bottleneck
Add per-endpoint and per-dependency breakdowns to isolate the cause

reliability.q: How would you define an SLO for a new service? What SLI would you pick?
reliability.source: Google SRE book (Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly), SLO chapters
talking_points: SLI: ratio of good events to total valid events, measured from the user's perspective
Choose the SLI users feel: successful requests, or latency under a threshold
Start conservative, exclude planned downtime explicitly, and revisit as you learn

reliability.q: What is an error budget, and how would you use it to balance feature work against reliability work?
reliability.source: Google SRE book (Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly), SLO chapters
talking_points: Error budget is 1 minus the SLO: the allowed failure rate over the window
Spend it on launches; when it is gone, freeze features and work on reliability
It turns reliability debates into a shared, quantitative policy instead of opinions

reliability.q: Design a system that survives the loss of an entire region.
talking_points: Active-active serving with stateless tiers and replicated data with known consistency tradeoffs
DNS or anycast failover, health-checked, with tested runbooks; watch for failover flapping
Regularly exercise the failover in game days; an untested plan is not a plan

reliability.q: Your service depends on three downstream services, and one is flaky. How do you keep your service reliable?
talking_points: Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, and bulkheads per dependency
Graceful degradation: serve cached or reduced functionality instead of failing
Set your own SLO based on what you control, and hold the dependency accountable to theirs

reliability.q: What is toil, and how would you reduce it for an on-call rotation?
reliability.source: Google SRE book (Site Reliability Engineering, O'Reilly), toil chapters
talking_points: Toil: manual, repetitive, automatable operational work with no enduring value
Measure the toil budget; automate the top sources or eliminate the work entirely
Fix the alerting first: noisy, unactionable pages are the most common toil source

note: Canonical SRE interview questions. Every entry carries a source label. Entries sourced from Google's SRE books cover topics those books genuinely discuss (SLOs, error budgets, alerting, postmortems). Entries labeled 'Reported SRE loop question' are standard questions widely reported from SRE/DevOps interviews. Nothing here is presented as asked at a specific company on a specific date.
